# Research Question:

What are the top 5 books that have been on the NYTimes Best selling books the longest?

# API Selected:

I selected the New York Times Books API. It is specifically the current hardcover fiction Bestseller List endpoint.

Endpoint:

https://api.nytimes.com/svc/books/v3/lists/current/hardcover-fiction.json

The request uses two parameters:

-   `api-key`: My authentication key, retrieved from my environment variable.

-   `hardcover-fiction`: The bestseller list requested, specified in the endpoint URL.

The API returns information about books currently appearing on the hardcover fiction bestseller list.

### *Approach:*

I started out by creating and account on https://developer.nytimes.com/. Getting an API key meant I needed to register an app. I named my app FavBooks. I wanted to get the basic requirements to start the homework out of the way, so after some refreshing on some of my skills, I was able to store the API Key in system environment and then load it here using request and req_url_query function.

```{r}
library(httr2)
library(tidyverse)
library("DT")


#Reading the Sys.env file where the API_KEY is saved
readRenviron("Sys.env")

#making sure the key isn't null
Sys.getenv("API_KEY") != ""

#getting the request ready, NYTimes gives example code for this!
req<- request("https://api.nytimes.com/svc/books/v3/lists/current/hardcover-fiction.json") |> req_url_query(`api-key` = Sys.getenv("API_KEY"))


#actually performing the request
resp<-req_perform(req)

#resp holds the actual json with results and books, untidy data
books <- resp_body_json(resp)$results$books 

#Creating a function to call run through each book, which will pick the
#called upon entity from the data
return_tidy<-function(x,field){x[[field]]}


```

```         
```

#### Dataframe creation using sapply function to run through every book

```{r}
books_df <- data.frame(
  Rank = sapply(books, return_tidy, field = "rank"),
  Title = sapply(books, return_tidy, field = "title"),
  Author = sapply(books, return_tidy, field = "author"),
  Description = sapply(books, return_tidy, field = "description"),
  Publisher = sapply(books, return_tidy, field = "publisher"),
  Weeks_on_List = sapply(books, return_tidy, field = "weeks_on_list")
)

```

### Top 5 books in descending order that have been on the list.

```{r}
 books_df |> arrange(desc(Weeks_on_List)) |>
  select(Rank, Title, Author, Weeks_on_List) |>
  head(5)

```

# Second API Call:

Making another API call to NYTimes that would return overview list. Upon investigating a little bit, I realized that it returns a list of lists (list of best selling books under Hard-fiction, or how-to books etc).\
I ran the following commands to investigate:

```         
books_overview <- resp_body_json(resp2)$results$lists
```

```         
names(books_overview[[1]])
```

Following code, returned a column name ***List***, which is NYTimes' way of showing genre, ***Average_Weeks*****,** and ***Number_of_Books.\
*** I felt like this data was more insteresting. and I decided to plot this.

```{r}
#| label: Trying API Overview Suggested In NYTimes API Help 
req2<- request("https://api.nytimes.com/svc/books/v3/lists/overview.json?") |> req_url_query(`api-key` = Sys.getenv("API_KEY"))

resp2<-req_perform(req2)

books_overview <- resp_body_json(resp2)$results$lists

books_df_overview <- map_dfr(books_overview, function(lst) {

  data.frame(
    List = lst$list_name,
    Rank = sapply(lst$books, return_tidy, field = "rank"),
    Title = sapply(lst$books, return_tidy, field = "title"),
    Author = sapply(lst$books, return_tidy, field = "author"),
    Weeks_on_List = sapply(lst$books, return_tidy, field = "weeks_on_list")
  )

})

books_df_overview |>
  group_by(List) |>
  summarise(
    Average_Weeks = mean(Weeks_on_List, na.rm = TRUE),
    Number_of_Books = n()
  )

```

```{r}
ggplot(books_df_overview, 
       aes(x = List, y = Weeks_on_List)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Weeks on NYT Bestseller Lists",
    x = "Bestseller Category",
    y = "Weeks on List"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

#Looking at why Children's books have such a huge >750 weeks streak.
books_df_overview |>
  filter(List == "Children’s Middle Grade Hardcover") |>
  arrange(desc(Weeks_on_List)) |>
  select(Title, Weeks_on_List)


```

# Data Cleaning:

The API response was returned in JSON format, with book infomation stored in nested lists. I extracted the *books* portion of the response and created a function called return_tidy to extract the data I needed i.e. publisher, weeks_on_the_list, etc.\
\
I also used the sapply() function to iterate through each book and extract it's rank, title, author, description, publisher, and number of weeks on the best seller list.\
\
I then used data.frame() to organize these extracted fields into a structured table with each row representing an individual books.

When I plotted the overview api call dataframe, I noticed that children's books plot was huge.\
It was \>750 weeks. I looked at the data (with the help of ChatGPT:\
***books_df_overview \|\> filter(List == "Children’s Middle Grade Hardcover") \|\> arrange(desc(Weeks_on_List)) \|\> select(Title, Weeks_on_List)\
\
***The above code gave me the outliers: WONDER and The Complete Cookbook for Young Chefs. Been the best sellers in their own categories for around 11 years.\
\

```{r}
ggplot(books_df_overview,
       aes(x = reorder(List, Weeks_on_List, FUN = median),
           y = Weeks_on_List)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip(ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    title = "Weeks on NYT Bestseller Lists",
    subtitle = "Focused view: 0–100 weeks",
    x = "Bestseller Category",
    y = "Weeks on List"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Conclusion:

It seems that Most popular books after the children type books are Paperback Trade Fiction.\
The analysis shows that the number of weeks books remain on the NYT bestseller lists varies considerably across categories. This suggests that bestseller longevity differs depending on the book category.
